title: Elijah was answered (1 Kings 18:36)
hookLine: Elijah's prayer on Mount Carmel came at the time of the afternoon offering
last: PRAY IN THE MIDDLE OF THE DAY.

cards: A mountain on the coast, three years into a drought. The ground is cracked. Crowds have climbed Mount Carmel to watch a contest.
On one side, hundreds of prophets of the god Baal. On the other, one man: Elijah. Two altars, two bulls, and no fire on either.
Whoever's god answers with fire, that god is God. All morning the other side calls out. Noon comes.
Nothing. Elijah waits, all the way into the afternoon.

teach.b: When it's finally his turn, Elijah does something strange. He rebuilds an old broken altar with twelve stones, one for each tribe.
He digs a trench, then has the offering drenched with water, three times, until the trench overflows. In a drought, he pours out water. No one can say the fire was a trick.
Then the verse that names this day.

In the old Jewish translation: "And it came to pass at the time of the offering of the evening offering, that Elijah the prophet came near." That's the afternoon offering, the same hour as Mincha. And his prayer is short.
In Hebrew, aneni, answer me, said twice. Fire falls, burns up the offering, the stones and the dust, and licks up the water in the trench.
The people fall on their faces and cry out: "The LORD, He is God; the LORD, He is God." Now back to yesterday's line from the Talmud.

Berakhot 6b says to be especially careful with the afternoon prayer, and gives this as the reason: Elijah was answered only at Mincha. The prayer that's easiest to skip is the one the Bible shows being answered.
One more echo. At the very end of Yom Kippur, after a whole day of prayer, congregations call out the words the people cried on Carmel, the LORD, He is God, seven times.
A mountaintop cry, said in late afternoon light, still.

how: Many Jews take the Talmud's teaching about Mincha seriously by gathering for it at work or setting a fixed time; at the close of Yom Kippur the congregation calls out 'the LORD, He is God' seven times, the people's words from Mount Carmel.

o: the long chant Baal's prophets raised all morning
answer me: Elijah's short cry on Mount Carmel
a psalm of thanks sung after a prayer is granted

games.q: on Mount Carmel — tap the pairs.

s: Elijah's prayer on Carmel was long and elaborate
it was short: hear me, O LORD, hear me.
Elijah had his offering soaked with water
three times, until the trench overflowed.
Yom Kippur ends with the people's cry from Carmel
the LORD, He is God, said seven times.

games.q: you're Elijah. it's a drought, and you need fire to fall on your altar. what do you do first?
o: soak the offering with water, three times.
games.why: he drenched it until the trench overflowed, then prayed briefly at the time of the afternoon offering.

practice: Elijah's prayer was two short verses, not a speech, so think of one thing you'd ask for, if you could ask, in the fewest words possible, and say it inside or aloud; if you pray, you can use his words, hear me, O LORD, hear me.
Then stop asking, and wait in the quiet after, the way he waited.

wordCard.voice: Aneni. Answer me: Elijah's cry on Mount Carmel, at the hour of the afternoon offering, which is why the Talmud says to treasure Mincha.

orig.note: Hebrew: answer me. Elijah says it twice on Mount Carmel.

carryVoice: Your line: heard in the afternoon. A week of Kaddish, mourners, Adon Olam, Yigdal, Ein Keloheinu, Mincha and Elijah. Six hundred nine days, done.
